## From first principles to writing your own tools

### PART IV — The Bioinformatics Ecosystem: Bioconductor · Modules 13–15

*Biostrings · genomic ranges · real file formats & a differential-expression taste*

Read a section, then do the matching exercises in `PartIV_exercises.R` before continuing.

## Where Part IV takes you

This is where R earns its place in bioinformatics. **Bioconductor** is a curated collection of 2,000+ packages for high-throughput biology — sequence analysis, genomic coordinates, RNA-seq, variants, annotation — all built to interoperate on a shared set of S4 data structures (the object system from Part II). Nothing in Python’s ecosystem matches its depth for genomics.

You built miniature versions of these tools by hand in Parts I–II: a GC function, a FASTA parser, a `sequence` class. Now you meet the industrial versions — `DNAStringSet`, `GRanges`, `SummarizedExperiment` — and a first real differential-expression analysis.

**Installation is different.** Bioconductor packages are installed through `BiocManager`, not `install.packages()`:

    install.packages("BiocManager")
    BiocManager::install(c("Biostrings", "GenomicRanges", "SummarizedExperiment"))

**Time guide.** Module 13 ≈ 6h · Module 14 ≈ 7h · Module 15 ≈ 7h. Total ≈ 20 hours. These modules require the packages above; if you cannot install them yet, read the theory and return to the exercises later.

## Module 13 — Biostrings: sequences done properly

Estimated: 6 hours. `Biostrings` provides efficient objects for biological sequences and the operations you wrote by hand, now fast and correct for edge cases.

### 13.1 The sequence classes

    library(Biostrings)

    d <- DNAString("ATGCGTACG")          # a single DNA sequence
    length(d)                             # 9
    reverseComplement(d)                  # CGTACGCAT  — built in, correct

`DNAString` is a single sequence; `DNAStringSet` holds many (like a parsed FASTA). There are matching `RNAString` and `AAString` classes. These are S4 objects — the `@` slot access and `setMethod()` dispatch you met in Part II are what make them work.

### 13.2 The operations you built, for free

    d <- DNAString("ATGCGCGTAT")
    alphabetFrequency(d, baseOnly = TRUE)   # A C G T counts in one call
    letterFrequency(d, "GC", as.prob = TRUE)# GC fraction
    reverseComplement(d)
    translate(DNAString("ATGAAATGG"))       # uses the real standard codon table -> MKW*

`translate()` uses a complete, correct codon table — compare that to the tiny lookup you built in Part I. This is the point of Bioconductor: the hard, error-prone details are handled.

### 13.3 Reading FASTA properly

    seqs <- readDNAStringSet("data/sample.fasta")   # a DNAStringSet
    names(seqs)                                      # the FASTA headers
    width(seqs)                                      # length of each sequence
    letterFrequency(seqs, "GC", as.prob = TRUE)      # GC per sequence, vectorised

One function replaces the hand-written parser from Part II — but because you wrote that parser, you understand exactly what `readDNAStringSet()` does and can debug a malformed file.

### 13.4 Pattern matching

    dna <- DNAString("CCATGCCCATGTAA")
    matchPattern("ATG", dna)        # all ATG positions, as an IRanges
    vcountPattern("ATG", seqs)      # count a motif across a whole set

## Module 14 — Genomic ranges

Estimated: 7 hours. A huge part of genomics is reasoning about **intervals** on a genome: genes, exons, peaks, variants, reads. `GenomicRanges` makes intervals first-class objects and overlap queries trivial.

### 14.1 IRanges — intervals on a line

    library(IRanges)
    ir <- IRanges(start = c(1, 10, 20), end = c(5, 15, 30))
    width(ir)         # 5 6 11

### 14.2 GRanges — intervals on a genome

A `GRanges` adds a sequence name (chromosome) and strand to each interval, plus arbitrary metadata columns:

    library(GenomicRanges)
    genes <- GRanges(
      seqnames = c("chr1", "chr1", "chr2"),
      ranges   = IRanges(start = c(100, 500, 80), end = c(400, 900, 200)),
      strand   = c("+", "-", "+"),
      gene     = c("rpoB", "katG", "gyrA")     # metadata
    )
    genes
    seqnames(genes); start(genes); strand(genes)
    genes$gene                                  # metadata column

### 14.3 Overlaps — the killer feature

The operation you would dread writing by hand — “which features overlap which?” — is one call:

    variants <- GRanges("chr1", IRanges(c(150, 2000), width = 1))
    findOverlaps(variants, genes)      # which variant hits which gene
    subsetByOverlaps(genes, variants)  # the genes that contain a variant

`findOverlaps()` returns the hit pairs; `subsetByOverlaps()` returns the overlapping features directly. This is the backbone of annotation: mapping variants to genes, reads to features, peaks to promoters.

### 14.4 SummarizedExperiment — the assay container

High-throughput results (an RNA-seq count matrix, say) come with row metadata (genes), column metadata (samples), and the matrix itself. `SummarizedExperiment` bundles all three so they stay aligned:

    library(SummarizedExperiment)
    counts  <- matrix(c(120, 45, 95, 88), nrow = 2,
                      dimnames = list(c("rpoB","katG"), c("ctrl","treat")))
    coldata <- DataFrame(condition = c("control", "treated"))
    se <- SummarizedExperiment(assays = list(counts = counts), colData = coldata)
    assay(se)        # the matrix
    colData(se)      # the sample table
    se[, se$condition == "treated"]   # subset by sample metadata — stays aligned

The guarantee: subset the samples and the counts, metadata, and gene annotations all subset together. This is the standard container that `DESeq2`, `edgeR`, and most of Bioconductor’s analysis packages consume.

## Module 15 — Real file formats & a differential-expression taste

Estimated: 7 hours. The formats genomics actually ships in, and a first end-to-end analysis.

### 15.1 The format-to-package map

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Format                  What it holds           Bioconductor package
  ----------------------- ----------------------- -----------------------------------
  FASTA                   sequences               `Biostrings::readDNAStringSet`

  FASTQ                   reads + qualities       `ShortRead`

  BAM/SAM                 aligned reads           `Rsamtools`

  VCF                     variants                `VariantAnnotation`

  BED/GFF/GTF             genome annotations      `rtracklayer` / `GenomicFeatures`
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The pattern is always the same: a reader turns the file into a Bioconductor object (usually a `GRanges` or a `SummarizedExperiment`), and from there the operations in Modules 13–14 apply uniformly. You do not learn each format’s byte layout; you learn which reader to call.

### 15.2 Reading an annotation with rtracklayer

    library(rtracklayer)
    # genes <- import("annotation.gff3")   # returns a GRanges
    # Then everything from Module 14 works: findOverlaps, subsetByOverlaps, ...

### 15.3 A differential-expression taste with DESeq2

The canonical RNA-seq workflow. You supply a count matrix and a sample table; DESeq2 models the counts and reports which genes change. The shape of the analysis — not a production pipeline — is:

    library(DESeq2)

    # counts: genes x samples (integers); coldata: one row per sample
    dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
      countData = counts,
      colData   = coldata,
      design    = ~ condition          # compare by condition
    )
    dds <- DESeq(dds)                  # fit the model
    res <- results(dds)                # log2 fold changes + adjusted p-values
    as.data.frame(res) |>
      dplyr::arrange(padj) |>
      head()                           # most significant genes first

Notice the ingredients are exactly what Module 14 produced — a count matrix and a `colData` sample table — and the result is a table you analyse and plot with the Part III tidyverse skills. The whole course converges here: base-R thinking, your own functions, tidy wrangling, and Bioconductor objects, working together.

Visualise the result the way you learned in Part III — a volcano plot is just a ggplot of log2 fold change against −log10 adjusted p-value:

    as.data.frame(res) |>
      ggplot(aes(log2FoldChange, -log10(padj))) +
      geom_point() +
      theme_minimal()

### 15.4 Where Part IV leaves you

You can now use Bioconductor’s core objects — `DNAStringSet`, `GRanges`, `SummarizedExperiment` — read the field’s real file formats, run overlap queries, and follow a differential-expression analysis end to end. Part V turns all of this into *reproducible, shareable* work: R Markdown / Quarto reports that regenerate themselves, and your own documented, tested R package.
